title: Bartholomew's Artistic Accidents
markdown:
Bartholomew the pigeon was the most dignified window cleaner in Sunny Meadow Market. He approached each pane with the solemnity of a surgeon and the patience of a clock. His spectacles never slipped. His grey chest stayed immaculate. He lived by routine, order, and an almost breathtaking fussiness about smears.

Today a problem perched in that tidy mind. He had announced a grand event for the square: an Artistic Illumination. The only wobbly detail was the artistic part. He had not worked it out beyond the sensible notion that clean glass would catch the light and that catching the light ought, surely, to count. He straightened his spectacles. A small fear ruffled him more than wind: what if they did not like it? What if cleanliness, his one true talent, was not art?

“It is a matter of radiant presentation, Pipkin,” he told his small assistant, who was pecking a crumb that had dared the swept cobbles. Pipkin’s eyes shone like marbles. “Light reflected. Magnified. The ordinary made clear.”

Pipkin nodded so hard Bartholomew feared for the hinge of his neck. Understanding, with Pipkin, drifted in and out like a light fog.

Theo the badger ambled over, nose twitching. “Artistic Illumination, Barty?” he boomed, cheerful as a kettle. “Sounds important. What can this old badger do for the illumination part? Is that French for very shiny, like a dropped button?”

Bartholomew smoothed a chest feather. “We require sparkle, Theo. A certain something. The stallholders have promised their finest crumbs if crowds come. If it is a mess, my licence may go.”

“Sparkle!” Theo’s eyes lit. “Leave it to me. I have a knack.”

He vanished into an alley known for forgotten treasure and returned puffing, arms full: tin cans that gleamed faintly, a shard of mirror that winked, and a flattened bottle cap with ambitions. He set them down with the pride of a curator. Bartholomew opened his beak to suggest arrangement, symmetry, perhaps a theme, and closed it again. Theo was already humming.

Meanwhile Pipkin, eager to help, arranged sunflower seeds and millet on a clean patch of stone. He nudged them into rows, then into a circle, then into something that might have been a star if stars were shy. He was not sure what the pattern was. It looked, to him, like trying. A crumb of millet stuck to his chest. He left it. Art, he decided, could be slightly untidy if the artist was small.

The square filled by degrees. A butcher paused. A pair of shoppers arrived with bags and opinions. Faces collected anticipation and a little confusion, the way puddles collect sky. Bartholomew stood on his small ladder, cloth folded with military care, and polished the bakery windows to a crystalline dare. Sunlight bounced and ran in bright scraps across the stones. He worked a corner until it squeaked, which he took for applause.

“Remarkable clarity,” he declared, wiping a stubborn jam ghost. “Observe the interplay of light and form.”

A young girl holding her mother’s hand pointed. “But Mama, he is just cleaning windows.”

“Yes, dear. See how the sun leaps, though? Rather pretty.”

Theo, taking sparkle at its word, piled his treasures by the old fountain in a heap that had more enthusiasm than composition. The mirror shard caught the sun and flung it into the eyes of a cart driver. The horse, Nellie, swerved with the dignity of someone who had not agreed to be part of a show. Carrots tumbled and rolled to the baker’s step. “Whoa there, Nellie!” The driver sounded more surprised than injured. He shook his head, blinking coins of light from his lashes.

Pipkin’s seed art, for its part, drew pigeons from every ledge. They arrived like an audience that had smelled the interval. They pecked with enthusiasm. Coos and flutter made a feathery racket that had not been on Bartholomew’s programme. A child laughed. Someone asked whether tickets were required. Bartholomew pretended not to hear, which is difficult when you are on a ladder.

A bead of something travelled down his beak. The crowd murmured, not with awe, but with good-natured puzzle. Theo’s shine was beginning to resemble a junkyard with feelings. Pipkin’s mural had become a buffet. Bartholomew hesitated on the ladder. He could climb down, fold the cloth, and pretend the afternoon had been only windows.

Then a large, bossy pigeon mistook the mirror for a giant seed and landed on the pile. Cans, caps, and glass clattered across the cobbles. The sound, in the sudden attention of the square, was magnificently ungainly. Dignity, that carefully preened thing, teetered.

He looked at his perfect panes, at Theo’s scatter, at the living storm of lunch. He could flee. He could explain, which would almost certainly make it worse.

He nudged his spectacles straight, hopped down, and ignored the gleam he had earned. He walked to a tin can and tapped it with his beak.

“This,” he said, “is not merely junk. It is a song the city already knew.”

Theo beamed, understanding none of the words and all of the praise.

Bartholomew turned to the feathery gathering. “And Pipkin’s Avian Palette is a mural that refuses to sit still. Seed and song. A collaboration.”

Pipkin puffed. Fellow pigeons offered appreciative coos, and also more millet. The crowd, which had been perplexed, began to chuckle. It was not the solemn spectacle of the poster. It was, undeniably, happening. Windows still threw their clean light. Theo’s bits winked like jokes that had landed. The pigeons bobbed, part of the show whether they had bought a ticket or not.

“Well, I never,” said the baker, flour on her apron, smiling as if a stubborn smear had finally given in. “It is rather wonderful, isn’t it?”

A stallholder who had worried about crumbs nodded, then offered Bartholomew a particularly fine one, which Pipkin intercepted with professional speed. Nellie accepted a returned carrot. Theo rescued the bottle cap from a puddle as if it were a medal and set it on the fountain’s lip, where it caught a last unplanned flash.

Bartholomew left the cloth folded on a rung and did not tidy the seeds. A sparrow asked him something official about illumination. He answered by watching the square hold sunlight, clatter, and the ordinary music of people deciding they were glad they had come. He adjusted his spectacles, not to restore a plan, but to see the mess he had agreed to keep. Tomorrow he would clean the bakery again. Tonight the jam ghost could wait.
characters: Bartholomew (patient pigeon window cleaner), Theo (badger friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
